marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q001.takeaway: The pneumotaxic centre lies in the upper pons; the medulla houses the pre-Bötzinger complex and dorsal/ventral respiratory groups.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q001.displayText: The pneumotaxic centre is located in the upper pons. Neural respiratory-control neurons lie in the pons and medulla: pontine centres are the pneumotaxic and apneustic centres; medullary centres include the pre-Bötzinger complex, dorsal respiratory group (DRG) and ventral respiratory group (VRG). The source diagram shows their opposing effects on inspiratory activity and output to the diaphragm, external intercostals and accessory respiratory muscles.

rationales.b: The midbrain is not the pontine respiratory-centre location specified.
rationales.c: Medulla contains rhythm-generating and respiratory groups, but the pneumotaxic centre is in pons.
rationales.d: The cerebellum coordinates movement and is not the site of the pneumotaxic centre.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q002.takeaway: Pre-Bötzinger complex in the medulla contains pacemaker neurons that initiate inspiratory rhythm and drive phrenic motor output.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q002.displayText: The pre-Bötzinger complex in the medulla generates the automatic breathing rhythm. Its pacemaker cells initiate inspiration and discharge rhythmically to phrenic motor neurons. Voluntary control originates in the cerebral cortex and descends through corticospinal pathways; automatic drive uses medullary pacemaker circuits and cervical phrenic and thoracic motor neurons for the diaphragm and external intercostals. Inspiratory and expiratory motor pools are reciprocally active. The source distinguishes initiation by the pre-Bötzinger complex, maintenance by lower-pontine apneustic stimulation of DRG, and termination when vagal and pneumotaxic input inhibits apneustic drive. Quiet expiration is passive; VRG is recruited for forceful expiration, summarized by DIVE (DRG inspiration, VRG expiration).
emphasis: The pre-Bötzinger complex in the medulla generates the automatic breathing rhythm.
Its pacemaker cells initiate inspiration and discharge rhythmically to phrenic motor neurons.

Voluntary control originates in the cerebral cortex and descends through corticospinal pathways; automatic drive uses medullary pacemaker circuits and cervical phrenic and thoracic motor neurons for the diaphragm and external intercostals.

rationales.a: Pneumotaxic centre in the pons modulates inspiratory termination/rate, rather than generating the automatic rhythm.
rationales.b: Dorsal respiratory group contributes inspiratory ramp output but the source identifies pre-Bötzinger cells as the pacemaker.
rationales.d: Apneustic centre is in the pons and promotes inspiratory activity; it is not the medullary rhythm pacemaker.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q003.takeaway: Pre-Bötzinger neurons fire rhythmic bursts to inspiratory muscles during quiet breathing; pain and cortical inputs can modulate them.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q003.displayText: The main respiratory-control neurons are in the pre-Bötzinger complex, on each side of the medulla between the nucleus ambiguus and lateral reticular nucleus. They send regular bursts through the phrenic nerve to inspiratory muscles during quiet breathing. Quiet expiration is passive and has no expiratory motor discharge. Pain can stimulate respiration; substance P stimulates and opioids inhibit pre-Bötzinger activity. Cerebral-cortex impulses also influence this complex.
emphasis: The main respiratory-control neurons are in the pre-Bötzinger complex, on each side of the medulla between the nucleus ambiguus and lateral reticular nucleus.
They send regular bursts through the phrenic nerve to inspiratory muscles during quiet breathing.
Quiet expiration is passive and has no expiratory motor discharge.

rationales.a: Quiet expiration is normally passive, so there are not regular expiratory-muscle bursts in quiet breathing.
rationales.b: Pain can stimulate respiratory activity through inputs/receptors affecting the pre-Bötzinger complex.
rationales.c: Cerebral-cortex signals can influence respiratory control, including voluntary breathing.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q004.takeaway: The upper-pontine pneumotaxic centre limits inspiratory duration and thereby helps set breathing rate.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q004.displayText:
The rate of inspiration is controlled by the pneumotaxic center.
Pneumotaxic centre:
Location: Upper pons (dorsally in nucleus parabrachialis)
Function:
• Transmits signals to the inspiratory area, i.e., it inhibits the apneustic center and thus the dorsal
respiratory group of neurons, to stop inspiration.
• It thus helps limit duration of inspiration and switching between inspiration and expiration.
• This has a secondary effect of increasing the rate of breathing because limiting the duration of
inspiration also shortens the duration of expiration, and hence, the entire period of respiration.
Diaphragm
emphasis: The rate of inspiration is controlled by the pneumotaxic center.
• Transmits signals to the inspiratory area, i.
respiratory group of neurons, to stop inspiration.

rationales.a: Cerebral cortex supplies voluntary modulation, not the automatic rate-control centre asked here.
rationales.b: Ventral respiratory group is recruited especially during increased drive/forced expiration.
rationales.d: Apneustic centre sustains or deepens inspiration rather than limiting its duration.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q005.takeaway: Apneustic input prolongs inspiratory ramp activity and increases inspiratory depth; pneumotaxic input limits the inspiratory switch-off point.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q005.displayText: Inspiratory depth increases when the apneustic centre delays the inspiratory switch-off signal maintained by the dorsal respiratory group. By contrast, the pneumotaxic centre limits inspiration by controlling the switch-off point of the inspiratory ramp. The ramp begins weakly and increases steadily, producing a gradual increase in lung volume rather than gasping. The respiratory centres control depth and rate by setting the point where the ramp suddenly ceases. The source contrasts pontine pneumotaxic modulation, medullary VRG drive for expiration, and DRG inspiratory output.
emphasis: Inspiratory depth increases when the apneustic centre delays the inspiratory switch-off signal maintained by the dorsal respiratory group.
By contrast, the pneumotaxic centre limits inspiration by controlling the switch-off point of the inspiratory ramp.
The ramp begins weakly and increases steadily, producing a gradual increase in lung volume rather than gasping.

rationales.a: Pneumotaxic centre limits inspiration rather than deepening it.
rationales.b: Ventral respiratory group is quiet during quiet breathing and is recruited for extra drive/forced expiration.
rationales.c: Dorsal respiratory group provides inspiratory ramp signals but the apneustic centre increases their depth by delaying switch-off.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q006.takeaway: The ventral respiratory group is largely quiet during ordinary breathing, then joins the dorsal group for extra inspiratory and forceful expiratory drive.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q006.displayText: The ventral respiratory group (VRG) is recruited for respiratory overdrive. It remains nearly inactive during quiet breathing, when expiration is passive and dorsal respiratory group (DRG) activity supports the basic inspiratory rhythm. During exercise or other increased ventilatory demand, signals spill over from DRG to VRG. VRG neurons contribute to both inspiration and expiration and provide strong expiratory drive to abdominal muscles during forceful expiration. The source comparison places DRG in the nucleus tractus solitarius and VRG in the nucleus retroambiguus; DRG supplies inspiratory ramp signals, while VRG is inactive in quiet breathing and active during forced expiration.
emphasis: ventral respiratory group (VRG) is recruited for respiratory overdrive
nearly inactive during quiet breathing
active during forced expiration

rationales.a: Pneumotaxic centre is pontine and modulates inspiration; it is not the medullary forced-expiration group.
rationales.b: Dorsal group supplies inspiratory ramp signals and is active in basic breathing, unlike the source-described VRG recruitment for overdrive.
rationales.c: Apneustic centre is pontine and stimulates inspiration, not the ventral group role in forceful expiration.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q007.takeaway: Apneustic-centre stimulation delays inspiratory switch-off and produces a marked increase in inspiratory activity.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q007.displayText: The apneustic centre is in the lower pons and stimulates inspiratory activity. It delays the pneumotaxic switch-off of the inspiratory ramp, increasing the duration of inspiration. Vagal afferents from pulmonary stretch receptors inhibit apneustic drive as inflation proceeds, allowing the inspiratory signal to stop and expiration to begin.
emphasis: The apneustic centre is in the lower pons and stimulates inspiratory activity.
It delays the pneumotaxic switch-off of the inspiratory ramp, increasing the duration of inspiration.
Vagal afferents from pulmonary stretch receptors inhibit apneustic drive as inflation proceeds, allowing the inspiratory signal to stop and expiration to begin.

rationales.a: The apneustic signal sustains the inspiratory ramp rather than decreasing it.
rationales.c: Pneumotaxic stimulation would limit inspiration, opposing the increased activity in the prompt.
rationales.d: The result is augmented inspiratory activity, not cessation of spontaneous respiration.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q008.takeaway: Mid-pontine transection plus bilateral vagotomy leaves apneustic drive relatively unopposed, producing apneusis with prolonged gasping inspiration.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q008.displayText:
Transection of the brain stem at the mid-pontine level with bilateral vagotomy causes apneusis.
At mid pontine level lesion, the apneustic centre is intact while the pneumotaxic centre is
separated. Concurrent removal of vagus inputs causes this kind of abnormal pattern of breathing
characterized by deep, gasping inspiration with a pause at full inspiration followed by a brief
insufficient release.
emphasis: Transection of the brain stem at the mid-pontine level with bilateral vagotomy causes apneusis.

rationales.a: Apnoea is cessation of breathing; the described pattern retains deep inspiratory efforts with pauses.
rationales.b: Regular breathing requires intact coordination of pontine and vagal influences.
rationales.c: The source defines the prolonged inspiratory pause pattern as apneusis, not merely irregular rhythmic breathing.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q009.takeaway: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond strongly as arterial PO₂ falls below about 60 mmHg, but respond minimally to PO₂ shifts in the normoxic range.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q009.displayText: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond minimally to PO₂ changes in the normoxic range, but their firing rises steeply when arterial PO₂ falls below about 60 mmHg. The carotid bodies receive very high blood flow per unit tissue, so dissolved oxygen can meet receptor oxygen needs in anemia and carbon-monoxide exposure even when total oxygen content is low. Peripheral receptors respond to arterial O₂, CO₂ and H⁺; under normoxic conditions ventilation is driven chiefly by CO₂ and H⁺. Their response to arterial PCO₂ is faster than the central response, while central chemoreceptors dominate the ventilatory response to increased CO₂.
emphasis: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond minimally to PO₂ changes in the normoxic range, but their firing rises steeply when arterial PO₂ falls below about 60 mmHg.
The carotid bodies receive very high blood flow per unit tissue, so dissolved oxygen can meet receptor oxygen needs in anemia and carbon-monoxide exposure even when total oxygen content is low.
Peripheral receptors respond to arterial O₂, CO₂ and H⁺; under normoxic conditions ventilation is driven chiefly by CO₂ and H⁺.

rationales.b: Peripheral chemoreceptors also respond to pH/H⁺ and therefore are not restricted to arterial PO₂.
rationales.c: Peripheral CO₂ responses are faster, not slower, than central chemoreceptor responses.
rationales.d: Central chemoreceptors are the dominant sensors for the normal ventilatory response to raised PCO₂.

rationales.b: H⁺/pH also affects peripheral bodies, but the question asks their oxygen-sensitive arterial variable.
rationales.d: Bicarbonate buffers pH and is not the direct variable monitored for peripheral hypoxia.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q011.takeaway: Cyanide causes histotoxic hypoxia and can strongly stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors despite normal arterial PO₂.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q011.displayText: Cyanide causes histotoxic hypoxia by blocking cellular oxygen utilization and is a strong peripheral-chemoreceptor stimulus despite a normal blood PO₂. Acidosis (increased H⁺) also stimulates peripheral bodies, while increased PCO₂ mainly drives central chemoreceptors. Carbon monoxide poisoning usually does not stimulate the carotid bodies because their high blood flow supplies dissolved oxygen even though total blood oxygen is reduced.

Acidosis (increased H⁺) also stimulates peripheral bodies, while increased PCO₂ mainly drives central chemoreceptors.
Carbon monoxide poisoning usually does not stimulate the carotid bodies because their high blood flow supplies dissolved oxygen even though total blood oxygen is reduced.

rationales.a: Acidosis stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors, but the source identifies cyanide as the powerful stimulus in this comparison.
rationales.b: Hypercapnia mainly drives central chemoreceptors via CSF acidification.
rationales.c: Carbon monoxide reduces total oxygen content while dissolved PO₂ can remain normal, so carotid bodies are not strongly stimulated.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q012.takeaway: Anemic hypoxia lowers oxygen content while dissolved PO₂ reaching carotid bodies remains near normal, so the bodies are not stimulated by anemia alone.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q012.displayText: Anemic hypoxia does not stimulate carotid-body chemoreceptors: dissolved oxygen reaching the receptors is generally normal even though total oxygen content is markedly reduced. The carotid bodies’ exceptionally high perfusion allows tissue oxygen needs to be met largely from dissolved O₂. Peripheral bodies respond instead when arterial PO₂ falls, as in hypoxic hypoxia, and can also be stimulated in stagnant or histotoxic hypoxia.
emphasis: Anemic hypoxia does not stimulate carotid-body chemoreceptors: dissolved oxygen reaching the receptors is generally normal even though total oxygen content is markedly reduced.
The carotid bodies’ exceptionally high perfusion allows tissue oxygen needs to be met largely from dissolved O₂.
Peripheral bodies respond instead when arterial PO₂ falls, as in hypoxic hypoxia, and can also be stimulated in stagnant or histotoxic hypoxia.

rationales.b: Hypoxic hypoxia lowers arterial PO₂ and stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors.
rationales.c: Stagnant hypoxia reduces tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery to the receptors.
rationales.d: Histotoxic hypoxia, such as cyanide poisoning, is listed as a peripheral chemoreceptor stimulus.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q013.takeaway: Central chemoreceptors respond to CSF pH: CO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier, generates H⁺ in CSF, and changes their firing.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q013.displayText: Central chemoreceptors on the ventral medulla are activated by changes in CSF pH. They do not respond to blood PO₂. For a given PCO₂ increase, CSF pH falls more than blood pH because CSF has less buffering; CO₂ forms carbonic acid, which dissociates to H⁺ and bicarbonate. CSF bicarbonate can buffer H⁺ and alter the pH signal and receptor output.
emphasis: Central chemoreceptors on the ventral medulla are activated by changes in CSF pH.
They do not respond to blood PO₂.
For a given PCO₂ increase, CSF pH falls more than blood pH because CSF has less buffering; CO₂ forms carbonic acid, which dissociates to H⁺ and bicarbonate.

rationales.a: Central chemoreceptors do not respond to blood PO₂; CO₂ influences them indirectly through CSF chemistry.
rationales.c: CSF has less buffering than blood, so for a given PCO₂ rise its pH falls more, not less.
rationales.d: CSF bicarbonate buffering changes pH and therefore can alter central chemoreceptor output.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q014.takeaway: Raised arterial PCO₂ is the strongest blood change driving central chemoreceptors because CO₂ enters CSF and raises local H⁺.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q014.displayText:
Central chemoreceptors are most sensitive to increased PCO₂ in the blood.
Central chemoreceptors are most sensitive to increased PCO₂ in the blood because CO₂ moves into
the CSF, where it is promptly hydrated to form H2CO3 that dissociates to increase the CSF H⁺
concentration. This stimulates the central chemoreceptors, which monitor CSF H⁺ concentration
(not blood H⁺ concentration).
Other options:
• H⁺ in arterial blood penetrates the blood-brain barrier very slowly and hence has little effect on
central chemoreceptors.
• Arterial PO₂ has no effect on central chemoreceptors.
emphasis: Central chemoreceptors are most sensitive to increased PCO₂ in the blood.
(not blood H⁺ concentration).
• Arterial PO₂ has no effect on central chemoreceptors.

rationales.a: Arterial PO₂ has no direct effect on central chemoreceptors.
rationales.c: Arterial H⁺ crosses the blood–brain barrier slowly, so it has less immediate central effect than CO₂.
rationales.d: A fall in PCO₂ reduces the CSF acidifying stimulus rather than activating central chemoreceptors.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q016.takeaway: Falling arterial pressure can raise ventilation through both hypoperfusion-driven peripheral hypoxia and CO₂ retention/CSF acidification centrally.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q016.displayText: Both peripheral and central chemoreceptors can increase ventilation when arterial pressure falls. Reduced pressure can cause CO₂ retention, increasing arterial PCO₂ and CSF H⁺ to activate central chemoreceptors; hypoperfusion also causes tissue/receptor hypoxia that activates peripheral chemoreceptors. A fall in PCO₂ or H⁺ would reduce rather than increase chemoreceptor drive.

A fall in PCO₂ or H⁺ would reduce rather than increase chemoreceptor drive.

rationales.a: A fall in arterial PCO₂ would reduce chemoreceptor drive rather than cause the response.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q018.takeaway: At rest, CSF pH acting on central chemoreceptors is the dominant ventilatory stimulus, with arterial CO₂ supplying the diffusible trigger.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH25_Q018.displayText:
The most important stimulus comes from the pH of the CSF on the central chemoreceptors. The
COz2 that enters the brain and CSF is hydrated to H2CO3 and dissociates, leading to rising H⁺
levels. The CSF H⁺ concentration hence parallels the arterial CO₂ levels.
The effect of PO₂ on peripheral chemoreceptors under normoxic conditions is very small. Changes
in PCO₂ do affect the peripheral chemoreceptors, but the magnitude is less than that for the
central chemoreceptors.
The effect of changes in the pH on peripheral chemoreceptors under normal conditions is small:
and the changes in PO₂ do not affect the central chemoreceptors.

rationales.c: Peripheral bodies respond to PCO₂, but the response magnitude is less than central chemoreceptor response.
rationales.d: Under normoxia, PO₂ changes have little effect on peripheral bodies; central bodies do not sense blood PO₂.
